comparator.name: Forest and Nature Conservation (Bachelor Bos- en Natuurbeheer)
comparator.sourceNotes: The current handbook defines a 180-EC bachelor with a 120-EC common part, one 30-EC specialisation and 30 EC of open electives. Society and Policy is selected by the official-order tie-break. The common part is reconstructed with the Wageningen location-dependent courses, Statistics 1, Research Methodology for Human–Environment Interactions and the 12-EC WUR thesis; the specialisation uses its Wageningen economics choice and the first listed 6-EC restricted option.

routeSelection.basis: The generic target has two equally formal specialisations, Society and Policy and Ecology and Conservation. Neither is clearly broader or less specialised, so the first current handbook specialisation is selected before considering UCR fit.

alternatives.label: Forest, nature, society & governance
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines ecology, biodiversity and environmental systems with policy, law, economics, social movements, communication, quantitative analysis and applied sustainability research.
alternatives.concept: A broad closest feasible response to Forest and Nature Conservation, combining biodiversity, ecology, climate and environmental systems with policy, law, economics, social evidence, governance and research.
progression: Ecology, sustainability, politics, mathematics and social-science foundations precede conservation, evolution, public international law, environmental analysis, advanced ecology, governance and research. All prerequisites and term offerings pass; six 300-level courses are included.

alternatives.label: Ecology, biodiversity & conservation science
alternatives.labelReason: Ecology, biodiversity, evolution, conservation, climate, soils, farming, spatial observation and field-based research dominate the validated schedule.
alternatives.concept: A natural-science route centred on biodiversity, ecology, evolution, conservation, organisms, climate, soils, sustainable land use, environmental observation and field-based research.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the broad closest programme, this route replaces its sustained politics, law, economics, sociology and communication strand with deeper ecology, biology, Earth systems, sustainable farming and environmental field research. It clears the 30-EC distinctness floor.
progression: Biology, ecology, sustainability and quantitative foundations precede conservation, farming, earth observation, marine biology, environmental biogeochemistry and field research. All prerequisites and offerings pass; seven 300-level courses are included.

alternatives.label: Nature policy, governance & societal change
alternatives.labelReason: The validated schedule is organised around environmental governance, institutions, law, justice, economics, political change and public communication, supported by sustainability science and data.
alternatives.concept: A social-science route focused on institutions, policy, law, environmental justice, economics, conflict, public communication and societal change in the governance of nature and resources.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the earlier programmes, this route replaces much of the ecology, organismal biology, conservation and landscape-science sequence with sustained politics, law, economics, sociology and communication. It clears the 30-EC distinctness floor against each.
progression: Sustainability, law, politics, economics, research and data foundations precede international law, public economics, advanced EU politics, governance, conflict analysis and applied sustainability research; prerequisites and term offerings pass.

core: Forest and nature conservation grounded in ecology, biodiversity and ecosystem functioning
Management and conservation of forests, landscapes, ecosystems, species and ecosystem services
Human–nature relations, policy, economics, organisations, law and natural-resource governance
Climate, water, soils, landscapes, spatial evidence, statistics and environmental analysis
Field, quantitative, social-science and independent research methods
A broad common foundation followed by a formal specialisation and open elective space
questions: How can biodiversity, forests and ecosystems be conserved and managed under climate change?
How can ecological and social evidence be combined in nature-management decisions?
How should conflicts over land, resources and ecosystem services be governed?

candidates.label: Forest and Landscape dual-degree context
candidates.reason: The current handbook confirms the Alnarp double-degree context, but the three-alternative maximum is already reached by the broad closest programme and the two named specialisation directions.

blocks: Both introduce the coupled ecological and societal foundations of environmental stewardship.
Both introduce biodiversity and its observation across organisms and habitats.
Both apply ecological evidence to conservation and management.
Both address environmental risk, adaptation and planning, although WUR is forest-management specific.
Both establish ecosystem structure and functioning as a basis for later conservation study.
Both examine water and environmental systems, though UCR focuses on adaptation in deltas.
Both provide advanced ecosystem-focused study; UCR uses marine systems rather than forest landscapes.
Both use field-informed interdisciplinary work; WUR has a dedicated forest and nature field course.
Both integrate evidence, stakeholders and governance approaches in sustainability practice.
Both develop spatial and Earth-system tools for environmental evidence.
Both establish Earth-system and landscape context for ecological study.

selection.assessment: The closest programme combines ecological and societal study. The two current WUR specialisations independently support a deeper Ecology and Conservation route and a Society and Policy route. All three are coherent, mechanically feasible and substantively distinct, so production stops at the maximum.

notes.text: WUR requires dedicated forest ecology, management planning, fieldwork and a 12-EC thesis within a 120-EC common core. UCR can combine ecology, environmental systems and governance into three defensible liberal-arts programmes, but it does not reproduce specialist forestry training or the same compulsory field and thesis structure.
